I think often we don't know how much of an improvement until after we see it. So I was playing DOA6, and I was thinking, man, Kasumi looks still the same as when she was in DOA1. Then I went back to look at some DOA1 replays on YouTube and Wow was I in for a surprise. If you put them side by side the graphics are on totally different levels. Why did I remember them being the same?
Our memory plays tricks on us. We may remember things differently from the actual truth.
I remember being blown away by the graphics of Final Fantasy 7 when it first came out. Now, I go back and look at it and it's pretty shabby, especially if you put it next to the remake.
So maybe today we think the graphics are enough, but maybe we will think differently when things go to another level.
BUT, some I must say being more realistic does not mean it is always better. Maybe for some use cases. For others, such as say pixel art, we don't need more polygons. It's fine the way it is. But if we were to say make an immersive VR game, then maybe realistic graphics is a lot more important.

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
I haven't been keeping up with the thread, but wanted to drop this in here anyways, for what it's worth.
Unreal Engine 5 performs like dirt. This technically isn't the fault of the engine. I don't develop on it, but from what I had heard from a smaller indie developer who is developing on it, is that the engine expects you to take advantage and heavily use their "Nanite" system which dynamically renders and culls polygonal data from objects relative to the camera port. According to that dev (and from my own modding experience) the classic way of rendering less data is LOD (low object detail - rendering an alternate version of a model that has low detail at a distance) and mipmaps (rendering a lower resolution of a texture depending on distance from object). However, Nanite effectively makes these old techniques obsolete.
Unfortunately, I think many games releasing using UE5 are not taking advantage of nanite as it is intended.
This is all hearsay, I basically just want to say; we've had a bunch of games launch this year using UE5 and they require a super computer to actually rasterize it effectively. Instead heavily relying on AI up scaling technologies, which...imo, I'd prefer true rasterization locally if I can get away with it, and then enhance what I can render with AI upscaling, instead of being required to use AI upscaling just to get reasonable performance.
I like graphics tech, but I like graphics tech I can actually run.
I hope this wasn't too off-topic.

posts.author: ZimXero
posts.body: Games have been pushing toward more realism since before Pong.  Unfortunately, modern games are pushing too much of their limited manpower at audio-visual asset creation, and their insurance policy for this big investment, is to create a vanilla "SAFE" game design.  The new games are not pushing the envelope of game play possibilities.  That is part of the reason many players (and designers) have oriented themselves toward the Indy game market.   Unless a landmark originally creative game design with mass popularity releases, or a global calamity occurs, I think this trend will continue for decades.

posts.author: brandonjadams
posts.body: Unreal is going to end up sharing something with RPGMaker, ironically - in the next few years as more and more indie devs start finishing and releasing Unreal titles, we'll see more and more swill with no gameplay worth mentioning, no story worth remembering, and dumb prices. They'll have great graphics (at least on the surface), but that'll be about it.

point: Unreal isn't necessarily the best engine.... it's just the one that puts more effort on being out there.
another point: an engine isn't more powerful just because it can render more complex graphics... an engine is more powerful when it can channel the power of the hardware it runs on, to the operator wrangling it, through the least cumbersome framework.
